newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian short-term rates not out of the woods yet.
newsitem.headline: Belgian short-term rates not out of the woods yet.

text.p: Belgian government bonds (OLOs) and futures and money market rates will remain under pressure for now, with those investors holding maturities of 10 years and beyond probably standing the best chance of preserving value.
The short end was hurt by continued dollar strength, affecting the mark and the closely-linked Belgian franc.
Elsewhere, in selected spots, the curve was hit by selling ahead of Tuesday's exchange auction.
Overal, the trend was one of curve flattening. "I would be very cautious at the short end, "a trader said. Speculation on German rate action to support the mark was largely discounted.

One-week repo rates edged up to 3.62/68 percent at 1500 GMT from 3.58/64 percent at 1200 GMT and 3.55/65 percent late on Friday. By comparison, the rates are now more than 50 basis points above the central bank's central rate .

Dealers were sceptical much could be done about the dollar's seemingly inexorable rise by dollar sales, mark purchases, and/or tightening liquidity, with some saying the U.S. currency would by itself become overbought just below 1.90 marks.
Meanwhile, speculation was rife the Bundesbank would act in defense of the German currency, engineering a rate rise by reverting to a floating rate money market repo this week.

One trader said. "The market is finally realising that the Buba might do something on Thursday." The Bundesbank might then announce a variable repo rate -- a de-facto rate rise -- or introduce a two-tier repo later this week.

Some traders said a move on the German repo was not fully priced into the Belgian market. "The short end remains very vulnerable. If the Buba does bring in a variable repo there will be a massacre," another said.
But a third said, "It is in the prices. There is a cushion." A move would at best have a temporary effect on the Belgian franc and the money and bond market.

At current market levels, even a 50 basis point rate rise would only take the repo rate, and the central rate if the Belgian National Bank followed suit, to 3.50 percent, leaving a 10 to 15 basis point gap with one-week repo rates.

Central banks in the mark bloc faced a dilemma, some traders said, in that any rate rises could damage the prospects for Europe's single currency union, giving fuel to the very reason cited as driving players into the dollar.
For that reason the banks were postponing action against the dollar. "No need to supply the speculators with cheap dollars," one trader said.
